title: Why Breaking a $100 Bill Makes You Spend Faster (Denomination Effect)
alt_title_1: The 2009 Cash Experiment That Explains Digital Overspending
alt_title_2: How Large Mental Units Stop Impulse Leaks Before Checkout
description_hook: In a 2009 Journal of Consumer Research study, Priya Raghubir and Joydeep Srivastava proved the Denomination Effect: people spend identical sums far faster when broken into small units than when held as one large bill. Here is how to rebuild that friction in a tap-to-pay world.

scenes.headline: Same $100, Completely Different Spending Speed
bullets: Five $20 bills vanish on casual errands
One crisp $100 bill creates pause before spending
scenes.narration: Hand someone five twenty-dollar bills and the cash vanishes fast. Hand them one crisp hundred-dollar bill and their wallet stays shut.
scenes.source: Raghubir & Srivastava, 'The Denomination Effect', Journal of Consumer Research (2009)

scenes.headline: Raghubir & Srivastava's 2009 Lab Proof
scenes.stat_label: SPENDING RATE: SINGLE $1 BILL VS FOUR QUARTERS
bullets: Breaking a whole unit triggers psychological friction
Small coins and bills feel already spent
scenes.narration: In a 2009 Journal of Consumer Research study, Priya Raghubir and Joydeep Srivastava named this the Denomination Effect: twenty-six percent of people spent a single dollar bill, while sixty-three percent spent four quarters.
scenes.source: Raghubir & Srivastava, Journal of Consumer Research (2009), Study 1

scenes.headline: Tap-to-Pay Turns Savings Into Loose Quarters
scenes.left_body: Tap-to-pay + 1-click apps -> zero unit boundary at checkout
scenes.right_body: Cash parked in $100 or $1,000 blocks -> breaking a unit stings
scenes.narration: Tap-to-pay cards and one-click checkouts turn your entire checking balance into digital loose change, erasing the psychological sting of breaking a large bill.

scenes.headline: Store Surplus Cash in Whole $100 Blocks
scenes.stat_subtext: Sweep surplus in $100-$1,000 blocks • Require manual transfer to spend
scenes.narration: Rebuild that boundary on purpose: sweep surplus cash into hundred-dollar or thousand-dollar blocks inside a separate vault account that requires a slow manual transfer.

scenes.headline: Make Breaking the Unit Hurt Again
bullets: Keep daily checking lean for fixed bills only
Never break a $100 vault block for trivial wants
scenes.narration: Once breaking a whole block feels painful again, impulse leaks dry up before you ever reach checkout.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin cashflow rule based on Raghubir & Srivastava (2009)
